title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

reading.body:
This incident shows a deliberate attempt to manipulate the training or retrieval pipelines that AI chatbots rely on for information. A fictitious organization produced a large volume of quasi-academic text in a compressed period, with citations to legitimate sources, specifically to appear credible to systems that index and synthesize published content. The failure mode is not one internal to the AI systems themselves but in the conditions they were built for: those systems assume that indexed sources represent genuine independent scholarship, and they have no reliable mechanism to verify whether a publishing entity actually exists.

The operation exploited a known gap in how AI chatbots handle source provenance. Chatbots that summarize or cite documents do not, as a rule, authenticate the institutional reality behind a named organization. Catching this would have required out-of-band verification, confirming that a think tank has a real address, staff, funding history, and track record before its output is weighted as authoritative. That check does not exist as a standard step in current deployment pipelines.

What is not established is whether any specific chatbot's outputs were demonstrably altered as a direct result of this content, or whether the AI companies involved were aware of or complicit in the campaign. The reporting describes the campaign's intent and structure, and researchers' assessments of influence on chatbot responses, but a reported observation of influence is not a controlled finding, and the accounts of Israeli officials acknowledging failure in public opinion terms do not settle the narrower technical question of what the AI systems actually absorbed.

reports.title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

summary:
# Summary

A fake research institute called the Hanover Institute, funded by Israel, published over 560,000 words across 124 reports in just nine days using a platform designed to optimize content for artificial intelligence chatbots. The nonexistent organization presented pro-Israel arguments on contentious topics including alleged war crimes, genocide claims, and starvation in Gaza in a quasi-academic format. The effort, which included citations to legitimate sources but framed information to minimize criticism of Israel, was part of a larger Israeli government campaign involving tens of millions of dollars routed through intermediaries including the advertising company Havas Media to influence what chatbots say about Israel.

The campaign included work by several American firms, including one run by former Trump campaign manager Brad Parscale, with total spending reaching nearly $25 million on American contractors alone. However, Israeli officials have expressed frustration with the public diplomacy efforts, acknowledging they have failed to improve Israel's standing as American support has declined significantly. Researchers note that while these efforts successfully influence chatbot responses, they have not changed public opinion polls, which officials view as the actual measure of success for the campaign.
